fields.meta_title: Lead Generation Landing Page: 4 Examples | Emergent
fields.meta_description: What a lead generation landing page needs, four worked examples by offer, and how each lead reaches the person who answers it. Free to start.
fields.h1: Build a Lead Generation Landing Page That Routes Every Lead
fields.hero_description: Describe the offer and who should follow up. Emergent builds the lead generation landing page with the form you describe, and saves every lead to a table with its source.
fields.features_heading: What Emergent Builds Behind the Form
fields.features_subheading: The page visitors see, and the rules behind it that decide what happens to each lead after the submit.
fields.feature_1:
Only the fields you ask for

Name the fields in your prompt, for example a required work email and an optional phone number. Emergent builds that form and nothing extra, and checks each entry before saving it.
fields.feature_2:
A lead table with the source attached

Every submission becomes a row in a database you own, stamped with its time and the campaign behind the visit. Filter the rows and export them, or sync each new lead to your CRM.
fields.feature_3:
Follow-up rules in plain sentences

Rules decide who answers each lead. Big accounts can reach one rep as a Slack message, and course inquiries a counselor by email. Write the rule in words and Emergent wires it up.
fields.feature_4:
Campaign tags kept on every lead

When a visitor arrives from an ad, the page reads the utm_campaign value in the link and stores it with the lead. Cost per lead for each campaign then comes out of your own table.
fields.feature_5:
Headline variants from one message

Send Emergent a message asking for a second headline or a shorter form. It builds the variant, splits visitors between the two versions, and records which one each lead saw.
fields.feature_6:
The page and its leads, exported

The page, its form code and the lead table export to your GitHub repository. Publish on Emergent under your own domain, or deploy the code on hosting your team already runs.

fields.usecase_heading: Four Lead Gen Pages by Offer
fields.tab_content_1:
Accounts over 200 employees go straight to sales

Tallgrass Analytics sells reporting software, and its demo page asks for a work email and a company size. A company with 200 or more employees goes to account executive Maya Chen as a Slack direct message with the lead attached. Smaller teams see a booking page and pick a 30-minute slot.
fields.tab_content_2:
One inquiry form, four admissions counselors

Prospective students at Brightpath Coding School pick a program and a start term on the inquiry page. Each inquiry lands as a row assigned to the counselor who runs that program, and the counselor gets an email with the student's answers. No inquiry sits in a shared inbox waiting for someone to claim it.
fields.tab_content_3:
A seven-day pass, claimed on a phone

On a phone, the Oakline Fitness page asks for a name, contact details and the home club. Submitting it issues a seven-day pass and emails it to the visitor. Staff at that club see the new pass on the front desk screen before the visitor walks in.
fields.tab_content_4:
Patio ads now cost $65 per lead

Each morning at 7 AM, Cedar Hill Landscaping's lead table pulls the previous day's ad spend and divides it by the leads each campaign brought in. Any campaign over $45 a lead is flagged. Yesterday the patio design campaign spent $1,560 for 24 leads, and the owner, Ruth Okafor, got a Slack message about it.

fields.howto_title: How to Build a Lead Generation Landing Page
fields.howto_description: A lead gen page earns its ad budget after the click, when a short form meets a person ready to answer every lead.
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Echo the ad in the headline
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Ask for the fields sales will use
fields.howto_step_1_des: Pick the single thing a visitor gets in exchange for their details, whether that is a demo or a downloadable guide. Two offers on one page split attention and blur your numbers. Running two offers means two pages, each with its own ad.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Visitors arrive expecting what the ad or email said, in roughly those words. Google Ads rates landing page experience partly on whether the page gives people what the ad led them to expect, and that rating feeds into a keyword's Quality Score.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Each field should change what happens next. Company size can decide routing, and a phone number matters only if someone will call it. Cut every other field, or move it to a second step that appears after the visitor has already submitted once.
fields.howto_step_4_des: A named customer quote, a row of client logos or a review count placed next to the form answers the doubt a visitor feels while typing an email address. Specific beats general here: one customer and one result outweigh a page of praise.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Write the routing down before launch. Say which leads go to which person and what the visitor sees after submitting. A lead left two days in an unread inbox is ad spend with nothing to show for it, and the visitor has moved on.
fields.howto_step_6_title: 06 Tag every link with its campaign
fields.howto_step_6_des: Add campaign parameters such as utm_source and utm_campaign to each ad and email link, then save those values with the lead. Analytics tools read the same parameters to report which campaign sent each visit, and your lead table will agree with them.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Judge campaigns by cost per lead
fields.howto_step_7_des: Clicks are cheap to count and easy to misread. Divide each campaign's spend by the leads it produced, then compare that figure with what a lead is worth to your business. Pause any campaign whose leads cost more than they return.
